idiom_name: typedef enum + prefixed constants + explicit conversion/validation helpers
implementation_notes: C has no type-safe enumeration: enumerators are int constants and an enum variable can hold any int, so the classic closed-class structure can only be emulated. The accepted realization is an enum (or a fixed-underlying-type enum since C23) for the names plus hand-written helpers - one formatter and one validating parser - with all boundary input checked before it becomes an enum value. Compile with -Wall -Wextra and -Wswitch-enum (or -Wc++-compat) and keep switches free of default so a new enumerator is at least a warning; treat the enum as a documentation-and-switch aid, not as a compiler-enforced set.
pitfalls: Enum constants are integer constants in the enclosing scope: arbitrary ints can be assigned to an enum variable and arithmetic promotes them, so a range check at the boundary is mandatory.
A `default:` arm silently disables -Wswitch exhaustiveness checking; only the warning flags stand between you and a missing case.

The enum's size and underlying type are implementation-defined (or fixed only since C23 with `enum Name : type`); never put a bare enum in a wire/packed struct - use a fixed-width integer and convert.
